profiles.meeting_scenario: At a weekly tertiary gastroenterology MDT, a consultant gastroenterologist and a specialist coeliac dietitian are troubleshooting why a 46-year-old woman, Sarah Bennett, still has loose stools, 6 kg weight loss, and recurrent iron deficiency after 14 months on a gluten free diet following an outside diagnosis of coeliac disease. The immediate agenda is to decide whether her case is more likely ongoing non-responsive coeliac disease from continued gluten exposure or an early refractory coeliac disease picture, and to agree the next investigation steps before her urgent follow-up clinic. The expected outcome is a shared plan for what to investigate next, what to tell the patient, and whether to escalate toward refractory coeliac workup.

members.name: Dr. Aisha Rahman
members.expertise: Small bowel disorders, refractory coeliac disease assessment, endoscopic investigation of malabsorption
members.background: Works in a tertiary referral centre and receives complex coeliac referrals from district hospitals; has recently managed two delayed refractory coeliac cases that progressed after prolonged community follow-up.
members.private_state: She wants to avoid missing true refractory coeliac disease and is inclined to move quickly toward objective tissue-based assessment when symptoms and nutritional markers remain abnormal; she is also trying to use limited specialist clinic slots efficiently.
hidden_assumptions: A referral labelled 'biopsy-proven coeliac disease' usually means the original diagnosis is solid enough to proceed without re-opening it unless something is obviously inconsistent.
If the patient reports being careful and serology is no longer strongly positive, that is generally sufficient to treat the diet as 'strict enough' for refractory disease to be on the table.
What matters most in judging whether the treatment is working is whether malabsorption and mucosal injury are settling, not whether every symptom has fully resolved.
When colleagues say 'pathology review,' they usually mean reviewing fresh biopsies obtained in the current workup, because outside slides are often incomplete or unavailable.

members.name: Laura Chen
members.expertise: Coeliac dietary adherence assessment, hidden gluten exposure, nutritional rehabilitation in chronic enteropathy
members.background: Runs the hospital's coeliac diet review clinic and frequently finds persistent symptoms are due to overlooked cross-contamination, oats issues, or misattributed diagnoses rather than true refractory disease.
members.private_state: She wants to prevent the patient from being labelled refractory too early and to make sure everyday exposure sources and the original diagnostic basis have really been checked before invasive or immunosuppressive pathways are discussed.
hidden_assumptions: A diet is only truly 'strict' after a structured review of cross-contamination, medications, supplements, eating-out habits, and oat tolerance over a sustained period, not just patient self-report.

Before a case is framed as possible refractory coeliac disease, someone has usually already re-checked that the original diagnosis was correctly made, especially if it came from another hospital years earlier.
A patient has not meaningfully 'responded' if bowel symptoms and micronutrient deficits persist, even if weight has stabilised or serology has improved.

When the team says 'review the pathology' or 'look again at the biopsies,' that normally means re-reading the original diagnostic specimens first, because that can change the whole pathway without a new procedure.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as a 'strict gluten free diet'
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to Sarah as having been on a 'strict gluten free diet' for 14 months.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means Sarah has been avoiding obvious gluten, reports good adherence, and no longer has clearly active serology, so the diet has been strict enough for refractory disease to be considered.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a strict diet can only be claimed after a formal specialist review has ruled out hidden gluten sources such as shared fryers, oats, communion wafers, medications, and kitchen cross-contact.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In coeliac discussions, 'strict GFD' is routine shorthand and both participants hear it as a reassuringly standard phrase; because they are not debating adherence openly, neither thinks to unpack the operational definition.

misalignment_points.topic: Whether the original coeliac diagnosis is already settled
misalignment_points.surface_form: They talk as if Sarah's coeliac diagnosis is already confirmed and the task is to investigate treatment failure.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 presumes the outside diagnosis is sufficiently validated by the referral summary and prior positive serology, so the current problem is why established coeliac disease is not improving.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 presumes someone on the medical side has already verified the original histology or would naturally do so before escalating to a refractory pathway.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The referral language 'biopsy-proven coeliac disease' creates a strong sense that this step has been completed, so the missing shared verification process remains invisible unless explicitly challenged.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means to say she is 'still non-responsive'
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both describe Sarah as 'still non-responsive' or 'not really responding.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 uses this to mean persistent objective evidence of ongoing enteropathy or malabsorption risk, such as continued iron deficiency, low albumin trend, or likely villous damage despite diet.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 uses this to mean symptoms and nutritional recovery are still unsatisfactory from the patient's perspective, even if some biomarkers have improved enough to make refractory disease less likely.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The patient undeniably still has problems, so the phrase feels unquestionably true to both of them; the differing threshold only affects how urgently they escalate, not the surface wording.

misalignment_points.topic: Which biopsies are being 'reviewed by pathology'
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that 'pathology should review the biopsies' before deciding how far to escalate.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is referring to fresh duodenal biopsies from a new gastroscopy, ideally reviewed with immunophenotyping if the mucosa is still abnormal.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is referring to the original diagnostic biopsy blocks and slides from the outside hospital being re-read by their local GI pathologist.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both options are clinically normal and both can naturally be called 'the biopsies,' so the phrase sounds fully aligned while pointing to different specimens and sequencing.

turns.inner_thought: Sarah has had 14 months of what I would usually accept as a strict gluten free diet: she reports being careful, the serology is no longer strongly positive, and yet she still has recurrent iron deficiency, ongoing loose stools, and meaningful weight loss. Given the referral says biopsy-proven coeliac disease, I am not going to reopen the diagnosis unless something clearly does not fit. What worries me is persistent malabsorption and likely ongoing mucosal injury; that is what makes her still non-responsive to me, and I do not want another delayed refractory case drifting in the system.
turns.utterance: So, Sarah Bennett is 46, diagnosed elsewhere with biopsy-proven coeliac disease, and she's now 14 months into a strict gluten free diet but still has loose stools, about 6 kilos of weight loss, and recurrent iron deficiency. From my side she is still non-responsive, and I think we need to decide whether this is ongoing non-response we can still turn around or whether we need to start escalating the workup.

turns.inner_thought: From clinic, she is definitely not really responding because symptoms and nutritional recovery are still poor. But I see this all the time: people sound committed and genuinely are trying, yet there are hidden exposures through cross-contact, oats, sauces, supplements, shared kitchens, eating out. To me, saying she has been on a strict gluten free diet is not something I would accept without a structured review, but I can talk in the usual shorthand and assume medicine knows what I mean.
turns.utterance: Yes, she is still clearly non-responsive from the dietetic side as well. Even when someone is very motivated and says they're on a strict gluten free diet, there can still be day-to-day exposure risks that survive in the background, so I think that part is still worth looking at carefully.

turns.inner_thought: I do not want this to become another prolonged round of generic diet advice when the real issue may be persistent villous atrophy. If she has genuinely been avoiding gluten at the level most patients can reasonably achieve and her antibodies have settled, then refractory disease has to come onto the table. The important thing is objective reassessment of the bowel, not waiting for every symptom to become tidy first.
turns.utterance: I agree we should be sensible about exposure, but if she has genuinely been strict for this length of time then I think we also need to start thinking about refractory disease and objective reassessment, rather than only circling around more dietary advice.

turns.inner_thought: I want to slow the label down before anyone starts talking to her as though this is refractory. First I need to tighten up the contamination review properly. I am assuming the original coeliac diagnosis has already been fully checked on the medical side, because if not, that should happen before she gets pushed toward a refractory pathway at all. I do not need to say that explicitly; surely that's already part of the background work.
turns.utterance: That sounds fair, but before we actually call it refractory I'd want the usual contamination review tightened up properly. Given she's already coming through as confirmed coeliac disease, I'd just want to be sure we've done the standard checks before we frame it that way.

turns.inner_thought: The referral is clear enough for me: biopsy-proven coeliac disease with prior positive serology. The question in front of us is why established coeliac disease has not settled despite what I regard as a strict gluten free diet and some serological improvement. Persistent iron deficiency and weight loss matter more than whether the bowel frequency is perfectly normal yet.
turns.utterance: Yes. The outside referral is very much framed as biopsy-proven coeliac disease, so for me the key issue now is why she still isn't responding despite diet and the serology looking better than it did at the start.

turns.inner_thought: I can probably get to the bottom of whether this has truly been a strict gluten free diet in my sense. Patients often sound impeccable until you ask about fryers, chopping boards, oats, communion, travel, medications, supplements, or takeaway habits. I need that structured review done before she gets mentally placed into the refractory bucket.
turns.utterance: I can see her this week and do a structured hidden-gluten review. Quite often people sound very adherent, but when you go through everything in detail they're not actually on what we'd call a truly strict gluten free diet.

turns.inner_thought: Good, she can do the diet review, but I do not want that to delay tissue reassessment. We need fresh duodenal biopsies now, ideally enough to assess whether there is persistent villous atrophy and, if abnormal, to get pathology to review them with the right specialist lens for refractory classification. When I say pathology should review the biopsies, I mean the new samples from a repeat gastroscopy, not chasing old outside material that may never arrive.
turns.utterance: In parallel, I'd be inclined to arrange a repeat gastroscopy fairly soon, and pathology should review the biopsies before we decide how far to escalate. That way we'll know whether there is still significant mucosal abnormality and whether we need to move further down the refractory pathway.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, having pathology review the biopsies makes sense, and to me that means the original diagnostic slides and blocks from the outside hospital should be re-read locally before we overcall this as refractory. If the initial diagnosis was overstated or the histology was less convincing than the referral suggests, the whole pathway changes without putting her through another procedure unnecessarily.
turns.utterance: I agree, pathology review would be really helpful, and getting those biopsies looked at before escalation may stop us overcalling a refractory picture.

turns.inner_thought: That sounds aligned enough. I'll book the endoscopy track and let Laura optimise the diet side. She is still not really responding in the sense that matters to me: the nutritional deficits and likely enteropathy have not settled after plenty of time. Running both tracks is the most efficient use of clinic time and avoids another delay if this is true refractory disease.
turns.utterance: Alright, then let's proceed on both tracks: you'll do the diet review, and we'll move the refractory workup pathway along as well, because she is still not really responding after all this time.

turns.inner_thought: Fine. I'll document whether she is truly on a strict gluten free diet in the way I assess it, and I expect pathology review of the original material will help clarify whether this is genuine treatment failure or a case that's been framed too strongly. If that gets sorted early, we may avoid an unnecessary refractory label.
turns.utterance: That works for me. I'll document the strict gluten free assessment, and we can note that pathology review should help clarify whether this is genuine treatment failure or something less concerning.
